did_you_know.text: Did you know? On the very night Haman plans to harm Mordecai, the king cannot sleep and orders the royal chronicles to be read to him.
Did you know? The chronicles reveal that Mordecai had reported Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king’s eunuchs, who had plotted to assassinate King Ahasuerus.
Did you know? The king discovers that Mordecai received no reward for his deed, even though his report had been recorded in the royal chronicles.
Did you know? That morning, Haman comes to the courtyard to ask for Mordecai to be hanged, but before he can speak, the king summons him inside.
Did you know? When the king asks how to honor someone he wishes to honor, Haman assumes he means Haman himself: “Whom would the king wish to honor more than me?”
Did you know? Haman suggests honoring the man with royal robes, the horse on which the king has ridden, a royal crown, and a public procession through the city streets.
Did you know? The king orders Haman to carry out all the honors he had proposed himself—but for Mordecai the Jew. Thus Haman becomes the one who publicly proclaims Mordecai’s honor.
Did you know? After the ceremony, Mordecai returns to the king’s gate, while Haman goes home mourning with his head covered—a contrast that highlights the reversal in their status.
Did you know? Zeresh and Haman’s advisers warn him that if Mordecai is of Jewish descent, Haman has begun to fall before him and will not prevail against him.
Did you know? While Haman and his advisers are still speaking, the king’s eunuchs arrive and hurry him off to the banquet Esther has prepared.
